lines: A Bloom filter answers a single question about a key: either maybe present, or definitely absent.
For a key that was genuinely inserted earlier, could it ever come back definitely absent?
answer: At any budget at all, an inserted key always comes back as at least maybe present.

lines: Run it for real: at every single bits-per-key budget tried, every key that was actually inserted genuinely came back possibly present, with not one false negative anywhere.
steps.takeaway: A Bloom filter never forgets a key it was actually given; a negative result is always proof of absence.

lines: Build that same filter again, but with a much tighter bits-per-key budget this time.
Does a key that was never inserted at all ever come back maybe present?
answer: Some keys that were never inserted do come back as maybe present.

lines: Run it for real: that tight bits-per-key budget genuinely produced real false positives, against keys that had never been inserted at all.
steps.takeaway: A positive result only grants permission to go look; it's never a guarantee the key is actually there.

lines: Spend far more bits per key on that exact same filter instead.
Does that genuinely change how often a never-inserted key comes back maybe present?
answer: Spending more bits per key lowers how often that happens.

lines: Run it for real: spending far more bits per key genuinely lowered the measured false-positive rate on that same filter, by a wide margin.
steps.takeaway: More bits per key genuinely buys a lower false-positive rate; it's a real budget, not a free setting.

lines: One real production system states an actual bits-per-key table directly, in its own documentation.
Does a small increase near the low end of that table buy as much improvement as the same size increase further up it?
answer: The low end of that table buys far more improvement for every bit spent than the same increase further up does.

lines: That system's own numbers state it directly: spending a small amount near the low end of the table buys far more improvement, per bit, than spending that same amount further up it.
steps.takeaway: Spending bits per key has diminishing returns; the first few bits buy far more than the next few.

lines: That same system's own documentation also states, directly, why any of this spending is worth doing at all.
A filter like this one can cut the number of unneeded disk reads a lookup would otherwise have to pay for, substantially, often by close to two orders of magnitude.
So here's the shape of this whole topic: a filter like this one never forgets a key it was actually given, so when it says a key is absent, that's genuine proof, not a guess.
A positive answer is the opposite: it only grants permission to go check further, since it can occasionally be wrong about a key that was never there at all.
Spending more bits per key on that filter genuinely buys a lower rate of those wrong answers, though with real diminishing returns.
The entire reason any of this is worth doing is that it lets a lookup skip opening most of the files it would otherwise have had to check.
